context.full_target:
A sphere-valued map cannot vanish outside a compact set. As approved by
the user on 2026-10-23, interpret spatial compact support as compact support
of a perturbation from a **fixed unit vector**, locally uniformly in time.
This is a disclosed nontrivial interpretation, not a claimed author-issued
correction.

Let \(n,m\geq1\) be integers and let
\(u:\mathbb R^n\times(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R^m\) be jointly smooth.
Fix \(q\in\mathbb R^m\) with \(|q|=1\). Assume:

1. \(|u(x,t)|=1\) for all \(x\) and \(t>0\).
2. The acceleration \(u_{tt}-\Delta_xu\) is normal to the sphere at
   \(u\): at each point there is a real scalar \(a(x,t)\) with
   \(u_{tt}-\Delta_xu=a u\). No regularity of the selected scalar is
   assumed.
3. For every \(0<s<t<\infty\), a compact set
   \(C_{[s,t]}\subset\mathbb R^n\) exists such that \(u(x,r)=q\) for
   \(x\notin C_{[s,t]}\), \(r\in[s,t]\).

With Euclidean norms and Lebesgue measure, define

\[
e(x,t)=|u_t(x,t)|^2+\sum_{j=1}^n|\partial_{x_j}u(x,t)|^2,
\qquad E(t)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}e(x,t)\,dx.
\]

The spatial gradient square is the Frobenius square, and
\(\Delta_xu=\sum_j\partial_{x_jx_j}u\) component by component.
Prove integrability of \(e(\cdot,t)\), differentiability of \(E\),
and \(E'(t)=0\) for every \(t>0\). No assertion at time zero is required.
context.conclusion: For every t>0, e(·,t) is Lebesgue integrable on R^n. The finite energy E(t)=∫_{R^n} (|u_t(x,t)|²+∑_{j=1}^n |∂_{x_j}u(x,t)|²) dx is differentiable on (0,∞) and E'(t)=0 for every t>0. In particular E is constant on (0,∞), with exactly this normalization; no assertion at time zero is made.

record.definition: u_t(x,t)=∂u(x,t)/∂t, the componentwise first time derivative.

record.type: family of componentwise spatial differential operators
record.definition: For each integer j with 1≤j≤n, ∂_{x_j} denotes componentwise differentiation in the jth spatial coordinate on R^n. Repeated subscripts denote iterated spatial derivatives, and ∂_{x_j}u_t differentiates u_t in that coordinate. Spatial gradients of u have rows ∂_{x_j}u; their Frobenius square is ∑_{j=1}^n |∂_{x_j}u|².

μ is Lebesgue measure on R^n, identified with the product of n one-dimensional Lebesgue measures; dx in spatial integrals denotes dμ. Euclidean dot products and norms are used in R^m and its finite matrix spaces. On coordinate boxes, μ is the product of the restricted coordinate Lebesgue measures.
E(t)=∫_{R^n} e(x,t) dx, with the ordinary finite Lebesgue integral, used only after spatial integrability for every positive time has been proved.

record.statement: For any measurable space A, measure ν on A, real normed vector space V (a normed additive commutative group with an R-normed-space structure), sequence F:ℕ→A→V, function f:A→V and bound b:A→R: if each F(k) is ν-almost everywhere strongly measurable, b is ν-integrable, for every k one has ||F(k)(y)||≤b(y) for ν-almost every y, and F(k)(y)→f(y) as k→∞ for ν-almost every y, then ∫ F(k) dν→∫ f dν (Bochner integrals). No completeness premise on V is required by this declaration.

record.statement: For every t0>0, let J=[t0/2,3t0/2]. There exist a compact C⊂R^n and R>0 such that C⊂(-R,R)^n, u(x,r)=q for x∉C and r∈J, and, with Q=[-R,R]^n, μ(Q)=(2R)^n<∞. Every positive-order space/time derivative of u vanishes on (R^n\C)×int(J). The functions e and e_t are smooth. For every r∈int(J), e(·,r), e_t(·,r), u_t(·,r)·u_tt(·,r), and, for each j∈{1,…,n}, the functions ∂_{x_j}u(·,r)·∂_{x_j}u_t(·,r), u_t(·,r)·∂_{x_jx_j}u(·,r), u_t(·,r)·∂_{x_j}u(·,r), and ∂_{x_j}(u_t(·,r)·∂_{x_j}u(·,r)) are continuous, vanish outside C, and are absolutely integrable on R^n. All these scalar functions are bounded on every compact space-time box Q×K with K a compact subinterval of int(J). In particular e(·,t) is integrable for every t>0.

For every t>0, E is differentiable at t and E'(t)=∫_{R^n} e_t(x,t) dx=2∫_{R^n} u_t(x,t)·u_tt(x,t) dx+2∑_{j=1}^n ∫_{R^n} ∂_{x_j}u(x,t)·∂_{x_j}u_t(x,t) dx. Pointwise, e_t=2u_t·u_tt+2∑_{j=1}^n ∂_{x_j}u·∂_{x_j}u_t. All displayed integrals are absolutely finite.
For every t>0 and j∈{1,…,n}, ∫_{R^n} ∂_{x_j}u(x,t)·∂_{x_j}u_t(x,t) dx = -∫_{R^n} u_t(x,t)·∂_{x_jx_j}u(x,t) dx; both integrals are absolutely finite.
